Background Information

Living wills: https://www.federalreserve.gov/bankinforeg/resolution-plans.htm

Macroprudential Policy: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroprudential_regulation#Macroprudential_tools

On first glance it seems that living wills are a perfect example of macroprudential policy: The explicitly stated purpose is to make all large firms more cognizant of the possibility of failure and to have bankruptcy contingency plans prepared. However, in the best current survey of macroprudential policy-making (the GMPI), they aren't included. From Cerutti, Claessens, Laeven (2015):

The GMPI survey is very detailed and covers 18 different instruments, of which we focus on 12 specific instruments: General Countercyclical Capital Buffer/Requirement (CTC); Leverage Ratio for banks (LEV); Time-Varying/Dynamic Loan-Loss Provisioning (DP); Loan-to-Value Ratio (LTV); Debt-to-Income Ratio (DTI); Limits on Domestic Currency Loans (CG); Limits on Foreign Currency Loans (FC); Reserve Requirement Ratios (RR); and Levy/Tax on Financial Institutions (TAX); Capital Surcharges on SIFIs (SIFI); Limits on Interbank Exposures (INTER); and Concentration Limits (CONC). In addition to using these, we define LTV_CAP as the subset of LTV measures used as a strict cap on new loans, as opposed to a loose guideline or merely an announcement of risk weights; and RR_REV as the subset of RR measures that impose a specific wedge on foreign currency deposits or are adjusted countercyclically.

Additionally there are the following categories (in addition to an "other" category): Sector Specific Capital Buffer/Requirement, Liquidity Requirements/Buffers, Loan-to-Deposit ratio, Margins/Haircuts on Collateralized Financial Market Transactions, and Limits on Open FX Positions or Currency Mismatches.

You could say that they were looking at over 100 countries and so they felt the need to have a strict classification system, and some policies, like the living will, slipped through the cracks. But I feel that what makes living wills (theoretically) effective policy is that if the Fed determines that a given banks' will isn't good enough, they have the ability to impose capital restrictions or other penalties on that individual firm. And so since the effectiveness (ergo the impact on the financial system) of the living will program really takes place on the level of a single firm, it implies that the living will program is actually microprudential policy.

But of course there's a reason that it feels like the living wills are macroprudential - they are requirements that every large banking institution has to adhere to.

Thoughts?
